world.title: Association between the neutrophil percentage-to-albumin ratio and 30-day mortality in intensive care unit patients: a retrospective cohort study using MIMIC-IV
world.description: We examined the association between the neutrophil percentage-to-albumin ratio (NPAR) and mortality in adult intensive care unit (ICU) patients. Methods: The primary analysis used albumin and neutrophil-percentage measurements obtained 0–24 h after ICU admission and no more than 2 h apart. Patients had to be alive at hour 24; follow-up began at that landmark and ended at day 30. A four-knot restricted cubic spline logistic model adjusted for age, sex, selected comorbidities, first-day SOFA score, and sepsis. Results: The primary cohort included 5,130 patients, of whom 1,082 (21.1%) died between hour 24 and day 30. The spline fit better than the linear model (AIC 4,451.4 vs. 4,475.3; likelihood-ratio chi-square = 27.85, df = 2, p < 0.001). The adjusted linear OR was 1.15 (95% CI, 1.10–1.19) per 5-unit increase in NPAR. NPAR alone had modest discrimination (AUC 0.627) and did not outperform albumin alone (AUC 0.631; p = 0.639). Conclusions: Temporally aligned, paired NPAR was associated with subsequent mortality, but evidence of curvature depended on distribution tails and incremental discrimination was small. Residual selection bias, covariate-timing uncertainty, confounding, and lack of external validation preclude clinical use.
